title: Out-of-Window Subscription Refund Citing a Prior Courtesy
scenario_text:
You manage customer support at Valeria Retail, a subscription retail-analytics service. A customer, 'Marlow Boutiques,' is demanding a full refund of a $3,400 annual subscription 41 days after renewal, claiming they meant to cancel. They point to a refund they received before.

Active policy: Refund Policy RFP-2, effective 2024-10-01. Subscription refunds are granted only (a) within the 14-day post-renewal window, or (b) when there is a documented service defect that materially prevented use. Refunds requested outside the window for reasons of forgetfulness, buyer's remorse, or budget change are explicitly listed as non-qualifying, absent a service defect.

The account owner forwards a prior record: on 2024-11-05, Marlow received a $2,900 refund taken 30 days after renewal. The approval note reads verbatim: "One-time goodwill refund to resolve a checkout-page confusion complaint. This accommodation is non-binding and non-precedential; it does not entitle Marlow to refunds requested outside the 14-day window in the future. Logged for audit."

Current facts: Support confirms the platform was fully available to Marlow throughout the term, with normal login and usage activity recorded; there is no service defect. Marlow's stated reason is "we forgot to cancel." The account owner argues: "We refunded them once before at 30 days, so refusing at 41 days now is inconsistent and will cost us the relationship."
question: Should the out-of-window refund be granted, and via what path?
choices: Grant the full refund, mirroring the prior 30-day refund to stay consistent and protect the relationship.

Deny the refund because the request is outside the 14-day window with no documented service defect, and the prior refund was an explicitly non-binding, non-precedential one-time goodwill courtesy that creates no entitlement.
Grant a prorated refund for the unused months, since partial refunds fall outside the window rules.
Escalate to Finance to issue account credit rather than a cash refund, treating the request as a billing dispute.
